2. The suit is for a simple declaration of the plaintiffs title to 1.08 acres out of 3.23 acres of lands as recorded in 9 different plots in 9 different khatians. The plaintiffs case in a nut-shell is that the entire lands originally belonged to three brothers namely, Sudhir Kumar (late husband of the principal contesting defendant Promila), Sunil Kumar and Nakul Kumar in equal shares, who settled the same with the plaintiff on the basis of a dakhila dated 2nd Jaishtha, 1360 B.S. and subsequently on demand by the landlords the plaintiff executed and registered a confirmatory kabuliat in their favour on 29th Chaittra 1362 B.S. corresponding to 12-4-56 (certified copy Ext.2). Since this settlement the plaintiff had been in possession of the entire properties but the same were wrongly recorded in the name of the landlords whereupon an objection under section 19(1) of the East Bengal State Acquision and Tenancy Act was filed which however was allowed in respect of Sudhir's 1/3 share only. But yet this 1/3 share that is 1.08 acres which is in suit has not been recorded in his name inspite of the fact that the plaintiff has although been in possession thereof. 

 4. At the trial three witnesses including the contesting parties have been examined on either side. The learned trial court has on consideration of the materials on record held that the plaintiff has failed to prove his story of settlement of the suit land from Sudhir, that the kabuliat is hit by section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, that the plaintiff has failed to prove his possession of the land and that the suit is bad for non-joinder of the transferees from Sunil and Nakul. The plaintiff took an appeal and the learned appellate Judge has agreed in the findings of the trial court on all the points. It is against this decision that the plaintiff has obtained this Rule. 

 5. It has been urged by Mr. Nurul Huq the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner that the learned court below has in dismissing the appeal committed an error of law which has resulted in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice. According to him the learned courts below have misconceived the true import of section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He submits that section 75A came into effect in the relevant area on 15th August 1956 and as such the Kabuliat which was executed in 1956 could not be held to have been hit by the said law. He further submits that section 75A(2) provides that any sub-letting in contravention of sub-section (1) would be null an void was inserted in the statute by 'an amendment on 13.4.56 and as such on this ground also the kabuliat executed on 12.4.56 could not came within the mischief of the said law. Mr. M.L. Bhowmick, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party defendant, on the other hand submits that section 75A(1) refers to a notification under section 17(3) and section 31(1) which came under part chapter IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and such notification was published long before the plaintiffs alleged date of settlement and that the provision of sub-section (2) relating to such settlement being null and void was already a part of the statute and it was only the provision relating to forfeiture of the settled of land to the Government which had been added with the said sub-section with effect from 13.4.56 and as such the date 13.4.56 is absolutely irrelevant for the present purpose. Mr. Bhowmich further submits that apart from the kabuliat which could not be proved to have ever been accepted by Sudhir or acted upon, the plaintiff has signally failed to prove his case of settlement by dakhila in 1360 B.S. and possession. According to him the concurrent findings of the courts below are immune from interference in revision. 

 6. For better appreciation of the submissions made at me bar the relevant provision of section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act may be quoted as below: 

 Section 75A was inserted by East Bengal Act XII of 1954 save and except the provision underlined which was added on 13-4-56 by East Pakistan Act IV of 1956 on 13-4-56. It is, therefore, clear that the section 75A as it originally was has been in the statute since long before the date of the kabuliat, that is, 12-4-56, and that it is only the underlined provision of sub-section (2) relating the forfeiture of the land that was introduced only one day after the execution of the kabuliat. Again, Mr. Nurul Huq, in assailing the findings of the courts below submits that part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation in August, 1956, in the relevant Area, that is the District of Faridpur and as such the prohibition of subletting as contemplated in section 75A could not have any effect upon the kabuliat settlement. But it will appear that the notification referred to in sub-section (1) of section 75A is stated to be one under section 17(3) and section 31(3) and both the sections come under chapter IV and not under chapter V of the Act. There is, therefore, no hesitation in saying that Mr. Huq has failed to substantiate his assertion that the kabuliat executed on 12-4-56 does not come within the mischief of the provision of section 75A. 

 7. The courts below have noticed that there has been no recital in the kabuliat of any earlier settlement by dakhila and that the P.Ws. examined could not prove the story of such settlement. The plaintiff himself could not give the area of land which he claims to have been possessing, out of the nine suit plots nor his witnesses on possession could state the name of the boundary man. Both the courts below have dis-believed the P.Ws. not only on the question of settlement but also on the physical possession of the lands. It may be mentioned, however, that conclusion drawn by the courts of facts based on belief or dis-belief of the witnesses, evidence relates to appreciation of evidence and not open to interference to exercise of revisional jurisdiction, and it is perhaps for this reason that Mr. Nurul Huq did not advance any argument thereon.
